drills.los_text: describe risk considerations for spread-based fixed-income portfolios

questions.stem: A bond's yield spread over a comparable government bond is most likely compensation for:

options.A: reinvestment risk only.
options.B: credit risk and liquidity risk.
options.C: call risk only.

rationales.A: Reinvestment is a separate consideration, tied to coupon reinvestment and the investor's horizon, and it is present in default risk-free government bonds as well. It is not what the spread over the government benchmark pays for.
rationales.B: Yield spreads for a specific bond issuance over a comparable government bond cannot be directly observed but are derived from market information. The spread is a risk premium above the default risk-free benchmark that primarily compensates investors for assuming credit and liquidity risks. Credit risk depends on the likelihood of default and on loss severity given default; liquidity risk depends on the ability to readily buy or sell the issue at a price close to fair value.
rationales.C: Call risk is not the main component of a corporate yield spread. An embedded call is captured separately through effective duration and option-adjusted measures; the spread compensates chiefly for credit and liquidity risk.

questions.stem: Expected loss (EL) under the credit valuation adjustment (CVA) framework is most likely computed as:

options.A: loss given default alone.
options.B: the probability of default alone.
options.C: loss given default multiplied by the probability of default.

rationales.A: Loss given default measures the size of the loss but says nothing about how likely that loss is, so it cannot be the expected loss on its own. LGD itself equals expected exposure (EE) × (1 − recovery rate, RR); the probability weight POD completes EL = LGD × POD.
rationales.B: The probability of default carries no dollar magnitude. It has to be weighted by loss severity, LGD = EE × (1 − RR), before it becomes an expected loss: EL = LGD × POD.
rationales.C: The CVA framework chains four steps. Expected exposure (EE) × (1 − recovery rate, RR) = loss given default (LGD). LGD × probability of default (POD) = expected loss (EL). Each period's EL is discounted at the risk-free rate, and the sum of those present values = CVA. CVA is therefore the present value of the credit risk embedded in a loan, bond, or derivative.

questions.stem: Ignoring the time value of money, a bond's one-period credit spread is most likely approximated as:

options.A: loss given default multiplied by the probability of default.
options.B: the coupon rate less the yield to maturity.
options.C: the probability of default alone.

rationales.A: The one-period credit spread estimate, ignoring time value, equals LGD × POD. Rearranging gives POD ≈ spread/LGD, which lets a quoted spread be read as an implied default probability. The approximation works well for bonds trading close to par. As default becomes more likely, distressed bonds tend to trade on a price rather than a spread basis, with prices approaching the recovery rate, (1 − LGD).
rationales.B: Coupon less yield to maturity only reflects whether the bond trades at a premium or a discount. It embeds neither a default probability nor a loss severity, so it is not the credit spread relationship.
rationales.C: The probability of default alone is missing loss severity. A spread must weight default likelihood by the loss suffered if default occurs: spread ≈ LGD × POD, so POD ≈ spread/LGD.

questions.stem: Over 1983 to 2019, annual credit loss rates on high-yield corporate bonds most likely:

options.A: averaged 0.05%, peaking at 0.41%.
options.B: averaged 2.53%, exceeding 5% in several recession years.
options.C: averaged 2.53%, never exceeding 3% in any year.

rationales.A: Those are the US investment-grade figures: the highest annual credit loss rate for US investment-grade corporate bonds from 1983 to 2019 was 0.41%, with an average of just 0.05%. High-yield losses averaged 2.53% over the same period, roughly fifty times the investment-grade average, and exceeded 5% in several recession years.
rationales.B: According to Moody's Investors Service, the highest annual credit loss rate for US investment-grade corporate bonds from 1983 to 2019 was 0.41%, with an average of just 0.05%. For high-yield bonds, the average credit loss rate over the same period was 2.53%, and in several years, usually around economic recessions, losses exceeded 5%. The gap in both the level and the cyclicality of losses is what active credit managers are paid to navigate.
rationales.C: The 2.53% average is correct, but the range is not. In several years, usually around economic recessions, high-yield credit losses exceeded 5%. Loss rates are highly cyclical rather than capped near their long-run average.

questions.stem: Over 1983 to 2019, the lowest volume-weighted average recovery rate on US corporate debt is most likely that of:

options.A: a first lien bank loan, at 64%.
options.B: a junior subordinated bond, at 14%.
options.C: a senior unsecured bond, at 35%.

rationales.A: First lien bank loans sit at the top of the capital structure and are secured, which gives them among the highest recoveries, 64% on a volume-weighted average basis. That is the best of the nine debt types, not the worst.
rationales.B: Junior subordinated bonds have the lowest volume-weighted average recovery rate, at 14%. The ranking from highest to lowest is: first lien bank loan 64%, first lien bond 55%, second lien bond 45%, senior unsecured bank loan 44%, senior unsecured bond 35%, second lien bank loan 29%, subordinated bond 28%, senior subordinated bond 27%, junior subordinated bond 14%. Position in the capital structure and secured versus unsecured status drive recovery, which is why loss given default varies so widely across instruments of the same issuer.
rationales.C: Senior unsecured bonds recover 35% on a volume-weighted average basis, below the secured instruments but well above the subordinated tranches, and more than twice the 14% recovered by junior subordinated bonds.

questions.stem: Credit migration (change in credit rating) is most likely:

options.A: irrelevant to bond prices.
options.B: negative for bond prices.
options.C: positive for bond prices.

rationales.A: Migration is a key component of credit risk, not an irrelevance. Although actual defaults are rare among higher-rated issuers, changes in the relative assessment of creditworthiness occur far more frequently, and they reprice the bond through its yield spread.
rationales.B: Although actual defaults are relatively rare among higher-rated bond issuers, changes in the relative assessment of creditworthiness occur more frequently. Credit migration, the likelihood of a change in a bond's public credit rating, usually has a negative effect on bond prices. This occurs because the chance of a downgrade exceeds that of an upgrade, and the yield spread increase at lower credit ratings is far greater than the spread decrease in the event of a credit upgrade. The expected price effect of migration is therefore asymmetric against the bondholder.
rationales.C: The price effect of migration is asymmetric and the downside dominates. Downgrades are more likely than upgrades, and the spread widening on a downgrade is far greater than the spread narrowing on an upgrade, so on average migration costs bondholders rather than benefits them.

questions.stem: Empirical duration, unlike analytical duration, is most likely:

options.A: calculated without reference to market data.
options.B: applied only to government bonds.
options.C: estimated by regressing bond returns on changes in benchmark rates.

rationales.A: Empirical duration is the measure that leans most directly on market data: it is fitted to historical bond prices and benchmark yields. Analytical duration is the estimate computed from a pricing relationship using duration and convexity inputs.
rationales.B: Empirical duration is used especially for high-yield bonds, not only for government bonds. High-yield credit spreads often show a negative correlation with government benchmark yields, a flight-to-quality effect that analytical duration misses; government bonds have no such spread behavior to correct for.
rationales.C: Empirical duration is derived by regressing bond price returns on changes in benchmark rates using historical market data. The observed negative correlation between high-yield credit spreads and government benchmark yields to maturity often leads fixed-income practitioners to use statistical models and historical bond market data to estimate empirical duration rather than rely on analytical estimates based on duration and convexity. The effect is large: for one high-yield bond, analytical duration of 4.234 compares with an empirical duration of 2.95, so a 50 bp decline in benchmark rates implies a 2.117% price gain analytically against 1.475% empirically, overstating the gain by $339,769 on a $50 million position.

drills.los_text: discuss the advantages and disadvantages of credit spread measures for spread-based fixed-income portfolios, and explain why option-adjusted spread is considered the most appropriate measure

questions.stem: The simple yield spread (benchmark spread) is most likely:

options.A: the spread over CDS market pricing.
options.B: the spread over swap rates.
options.C: the spread over an on-the-run government bond of similar maturity.

rationales.A: A spread measured against CDS market pricing is the CDS basis, which compares cash bond spreads with the cost of synthetic protection rather than with a government benchmark yield.
rationales.B: A spread quoted over swap rates is the interpolated spread, or I-spread, which references the swap curve instead of the government curve.
rationales.C: The yield spread, or benchmark spread, is the simple difference between a bond's yield to maturity and the yield to maturity of an on-the-run government bond of similar maturity. Its advantage is that it is simple to calculate and observe. Its disadvantages are maturity mismatch against the chosen benchmark, bias from the slope of the yield curve, and inconsistency over time, because the government benchmark changes as the bond nears maturity.

questions.stem: The G-spread is most likely:

options.A: the yield spread to a single benchmark government bond.
options.B: the spread over the interpolated swap rate.
options.C: the spread over interpolated government yields.

rationales.A: The yield spread is simply the difference between the bond's yield to maturity and that of a single benchmark government bond. The G-spread instead interpolates between two government YTMs to match the bond's maturity, which is precisely its advantage: it removes the maturity mismatch the yield spread leaves in place. The two measures coincide only when the government curve happens to be flat across the relevant maturities; otherwise they differ.
rationales.B: The spread over swap rates is the I-spread, whose benchmark is the swap fixed rate derived from MRRs and interpolated to the bond's tenor. The G-spread's benchmark is the government bond curve, not the swap curve.
rationales.C: The G-spread is the spread over an interpolated government bond yield, built from constant maturity Treasury YTMs so that the benchmark matches the bond's maturity. For a bank bond with an 8-year maturity and a YTM of 2.68%, interpolating the 7-year government YTM of 1.39% and the 10-year of 1.66% with weights of 66.7% and 33.3% gives an interpolated 8-year government rate of 1.48%, so the G-spread is 2.68% - 1.48% = 1.20%. Its advantages are transparency and a maturity-matched, default-risk-free benchmark; its drawback is that it is subject to changes in demand for government bonds.

questions.stem: The I-spread (interpolated spread) is most likely:

options.A: the spread over an interpolated swap rate of matching tenor.
options.B: the difference between government and Treasury yields.
options.C: the CDS basis.

rationales.A: The I-spread uses interest rate swaps as its benchmark, taking the swap fixed rate interpolated to the bond's tenor; swap rates are themselves derived from MRRs. Its advantages are that it measures the bond against a market-based (MRR) benchmark often used as a hedge or in a carry trade, and that it can be used across all maturities because swaps are quoted at all tenors. Its disadvantages are that it is a point estimate of the term structure and that, as a credit risk measure, it is limited to option-free bonds.
rationales.B: Government bonds and Treasuries are the same class of default-risk-free instrument, so there is no spread between them to interpolate. The I-spread is measured against the swap curve, not against a government curve at all.
rationales.C: The CDS basis is the difference between an issuer's credit default swap spread and the spread on its cash bonds, a comparison drawn from the credit derivatives market. The I-spread is a cash bond's yield measured against an interpolated swap fixed rate of matching tenor.

questions.stem: The asset swap spread (ASW) is most likely:

options.A: the same measure as the bond's Z-spread, differing only in name.
options.B: the bond's coupon rate less the matched swap fixed rate.
options.C: the issuer's CDS spread quoted in the derivatives market.

rationales.A: The Z-spread is a constant spread added to every point of the zero (spot) curve. The asset swap spread references the fixed rate on a swap versus MRR against the bond's own coupon rate over its remaining coupon dates. These are two different constructions, so the measures are not equal by definition, and only coincide by accident.
rationales.B: The asset swap spread is the difference between the bond's fixed coupon rate and the fixed rate on an interest rate swap versus MRR that matches the coupon dates for the remaining life of the bond. If the bond is purchased at par, the asset swap transforms the fixed-rate coupon into an equivalent spread over MRR for the life of the bond, so the spread then approximately equals the compensation for credit risk over MRR. For a bank bond with a 2.75% coupon against an 8-year swap rate of 1.647%, the ASW is 2.75% - 1.647% = 1.103%, or 110.3 bps. Note that if the bond defaults, the asset manager still faces mark-to-market settlement of the swap.
rationales.C: CDS spreads are quoted in the credit derivatives market on a contract referencing the issuer. The asset swap spread is a cash-bond-versus-swap construct, built from the bond's own coupon rate and a matched swap fixed rate.

questions.stem: The Z-spread (zero-volatility spread) is most likely:

options.A: the simple yield spread of the bond over a single benchmark government bond.
options.B: the part of the bond's spread attributable to interest rate volatility.
options.C: a constant spread over the spot curve that equates price to present value.

rationales.A: The yield spread uses a single benchmark point, one government bond's yield to maturity. The Z-spread is a constant addition to every spot rate along the curve, which is why it captures the whole term structure of zero rates rather than one point on it.
rationales.B: Zero-volatility means volatility is assumed away rather than measured: the Z-spread is the one constant spread which, added to each spot rate, discounts the bond's cash flows back to its market price. The spread that reflects an assumed level of interest rate volatility is the option-adjusted spread, which differs from the Z-spread by the value of the embedded option.
rationales.C: The Z-spread is a constant spread over a government (or interest rate swap) spot curve, added to each spot rate, such that the present value of the bond's cash flows equals the bond price: PV = sum of PMT/(1 + z_i + Z)^i plus FV/(1 + z_N + Z)^N, where the benchmark spot rates z_1 through z_N are derived from the swap or government yield curve and Z is the constant spread per period. Because it uses the entire curve, it is more accurate than the G-spread or the I-spread; it is also more complex, and as a credit risk measure it is limited to option-free bonds.

questions.stem: The option-adjusted spread (OAS) is most likely:

options.A: a measure defined only for callable bonds.
options.B: the Z-spread for every bond, with or without embedded options.
options.C: a generalization of the Z-spread that incorporates option pricing.

rationales.A: The OAS generalizes across option-free, callable, putable, and structured instruments, and that generality is the point of it: it is what allows credit risk spreads to be compared consistently on bonds with and without embedded options.
rationales.B: The Z-spread equals the OAS only for an option-free bond, which is the OAS computed under an assumption of zero volatility. Once a bond carries an embedded option, the value of that option drives the two measures apart.
rationales.C: The option-adjusted spread is a generalization of the Z-spread calculation that incorporates bond option pricing based on an assumed level of interest rate volatility. It is the constant yield spread over the zero curve that makes the arbitrage-free value of a bond with embedded options equal to its market price. The Z-spread for an option-free bond is simply its OAS, assuming zero volatility. Because it accounts for the option, the OAS provides a consistent basis for comparing credit risk yield spreads across option-free, callable, putable, and structured fixed-income instruments.

questions.stem: OAS is the most appropriate yield spread measure for active fixed-income portfolio managers most likely because:

options.A: it compares credit risk across bond structures.
options.B: it ignores interest rate volatility entirely.
options.C: it is the simplest spread measure to compute.

rationales.A: The OAS approach is the most appropriate yield spread measure for active fixed-income portfolio managers because it provides a consistent basis for comparing credit risk yield spreads for option-free, callable, putable, and structured fixed-income instruments. OAS calculations rely on models incorporating the current term structure, interest rate volatility, term structure model factors, and the specific option-based features of the bond. The main drawback is that the result is highly dependent on volatility and other model assumptions; for structured instruments, returns are also highly dependent on prepayment versus extension risk.
rationales.B: The OAS incorporates assumed interest rate volatility through its option pricing step. Ignoring volatility is the Z-spread's limitation, and it is why the Z-spread equals the OAS only for an option-free bond.
rationales.C: The OAS is among the most complex spread measures to compute, requiring a term structure model, a volatility assumption, and a valuation of the embedded option. Its value to a manager is comparability across structures, not simplicity.

questions.stem: For a floating-rate note (FRN), the discount margin (DM) on a rate reset date is most likely:

options.A: the spread over MRR that prices the note at par.
options.B: the quoted margin, fixed in the note's terms at issuance.
options.C: the note's fixed coupon rate.

rationales.A: The discount margin is the yield spread versus MRR such that the FRN is priced at par on a rate reset date. If the issuer's credit risk is unchanged from issuance, the discount margin equals the quoted margin and the note prices at par. If the issuer's credit deteriorates, the DM rises above the QM and the note trades at a discount (PV < FV); if the issuer's credit improves, the DM falls below the QM and the note trades at a premium (PV > FV). The zero-discount margin is a more precise version of the measure, taken as a spread over the whole forward MRR curve rather than a single rate.
rationales.B: The quoted margin is fixed at issuance and written into the note's terms, while the discount margin moves with the issuer's credit risk. The two are equal only in the particular case where credit risk is unchanged and the note therefore prices at par.
rationales.C: An FRN's coupon resets with MRR rather than being fixed, and the discount margin is a spread added to MRR, not a coupon rate in its own right.

drills.los_text: discuss bottom-up approaches to credit strategies

questions.stem: An investor using a bottom-up credit approach most likely:

options.A: allocates by sector aggregates without evaluating individual issuers.
options.B: focuses only on macroeconomic factors such as growth and policy rates.
options.C: compares each issuer's credit risk with the spread it offers.

rationales.A: Comparing issuers within sectors of comparable companies is the essence of a bottom-up approach. Allocating on sector aggregates alone, with no view on the individual issuer, is not a bottom-up approach at all.
rationales.B: Macro-first analysis, built on growth, inflation, and policy rates, is the top-down approach. A bottom-up approach begins from the issuer and its financial statements.
rationales.C: Once the credit universe has been divided into sectors of comparable companies and prospective bonds identified, the investor evaluates each issuer's implied credit risk by comparing company-specific financial information with the spread-related compensation for assuming default, credit migration, and liquidity risks. Beyond the prospects within a company's industry, its competitive position within that industry, and its operating history, financial ratios are a valuable tool for comparing creditworthiness across firms.

questions.stem: In comparing creditworthiness across issuers, a bottom-up credit analyst is least likely to use:

options.A: EBITDA/total assets.
options.B: Price-to-earnings.
options.C: Debt/capital and EBITDA/interest expense.

rationales.A: EBITDA/total assets is one of the three key credit ratios: the profitability and cash flow measure.
rationales.B: The price-to-earnings ratio is an equity valuation ratio, not a credit ratio, and says nothing about an issuer's capacity to service its debt. The three key ratios for bottom-up credit analysis are EBITDA/total assets, measuring profitability and cash flow; debt/capital, measuring leverage, the fraction of capital financed with debt; and EBITDA/interest expense, measuring coverage, the cash flow available to service debt. The advantage of financial ratios is comparability across firms; the disadvantages are their historical nature and the difficulty of comparing them across industries.
rationales.C: Debt/capital (leverage) and EBITDA/interest expense (coverage) are two of the three key credit ratios.

questions.stem: Reduced form credit models are most likely:

options.A: models of default inferred from equity prices and the volatility of assets.
options.B: models of default intensity fitted to financial and macroeconomic data.
options.C: models of default based on qualitative analyst judgment alone.

rationales.A: Inferring default from equity prices and the volatility of asset value describes structural models, which treat equity as a call option on the firm's assets. Reduced form models do not model the balance sheet that way; they take observable company-specific and macroeconomic variables as their inputs.
rationales.B: Reduced form models solve for default intensity, the probability of default over a specific time period, using observable company-specific variables such as financial ratios and recovery assumptions as well as macroeconomic variables, including economic growth and market volatility measures. Altman's 1968 Z-score is an early example: it combined liquidity (working capital/total assets), profitability (retained earnings/total assets), asset efficiency (EBIT/total assets), market versus book equity, and asset turnover (sales/total assets) into a composite score that classified manufacturing firms as likely to remain solvent or to go bankrupt.
rationales.C: Reduced form models are quantitative: they solve for default intensity from observable company variables such as financial ratios, together with recovery and macroeconomic inputs. Analyst judgment is not what defines them.

questions.stem: Structural credit models are most likely to:

options.A: rely only on financial ratios.
options.B: omit a default threshold.
options.C: estimate asset value from market-based variables.

rationales.A: Relying only on accounting ratios describes the reduced-form approach, which regresses historical default experience on company-specific variables (leverage, coverage, profitability) and macroeconomic conditions. Structural models are built instead on market-based inputs: the market value of the issuer's assets and the volatility of that asset value, derived from observable equity prices and equity volatility.
rationales.B: A default threshold is central to the structural approach, not absent from it. The threshold is the point at which the market value of the issuer's assets falls below the value of its liabilities; the probability of default is the probability that the asset value distribution crosses that point over the horizon. Without a threshold there would be nothing for the asset value distribution to be measured against.
rationales.C: Structural credit models use market-based variables to estimate the market value of an issuer's assets and the volatility of asset value. The likelihood of default is defined as the probability of the asset value falling below that of liabilities. Both Moody's Analytics Expected Default Frequency (EDF) and Bloomberg's Default Risk (DRSK) are structural models that provide daily probability-of-default estimates on this basis. They are sometimes called 'distance to default' models, because a probability distribution determines how far an issuer's current market value of assets sits from the default threshold.

questions.stem: In a structural credit model, an increase in the issuer's stock price volatility would most likely:

options.A: leave the probability of default unchanged.
options.B: decrease the probability of default.
options.C: increase the probability of default.

rationales.A: Equity volatility is a critical structural-model input, not a neutral one: it is what drives the width of the estimated asset-value distribution. Holding it fixed would leave the model with no way to measure how far the issuer's asset value is from the default threshold, so volatility cannot be irrelevant to the probability of default.
rationales.B: This has the direction backwards. Higher volatility widens the distribution of asset values, raising rather than lowering the chance that asset value falls below the default threshold over the horizon. Inputs that reduce the modeled probability of default work the other way: a higher coverage ratio, meaning greater cash flow relative to debt service, or a decrease in the leverage ratio, meaning less debt relative to equity.
rationales.C: Higher equity volatility increases the likelihood that the market value of the issuer's assets will fall below the default threshold. Structural models use asset volatility, inferred from equity volatility, to determine the likelihood of reaching the default point: a wider asset-value distribution puts more probability mass below the threshold, so the modeled probability of default rises. By contrast, a higher coverage ratio (higher cash flow relative to interest obligations) implies an improved ability to service debt and a lower probability of default, and a decrease in the leverage ratio (less debt versus equity) reduces the likelihood of financial distress.

questions.stem: A manager compares two A2/A+ rated pharmaceutical issuers, LLY and BMS, and finds that the market prices slightly greater credit risk for BMS only at the 5-year and near-30-year maturities. Their spread curves are most likely:

options.A: closely aligned, with BMS about 10 bps wider at those maturities.
options.B: closely aligned, with LLY about 10 bps wider at those maturities.
options.C: parallel, with BMS about 50 bps wider at all maturities.

rationales.A: The two issuers' spread curves are closely aligned except in roughly 5-year and near-30-year maturities, where BMS spreads are approximately 10 bps wider than those of LLY. If the bonds have similar features and liquidity, a manager might conclude that the market perceives BMS credit risk as slightly higher than LLY credit risk at those points on the curve. If the manager instead believes BMS is the stronger credit, several actions follow depending on portfolio objectives: overweighting BMS and underweighting LLY in cash bonds, or expressing the view through a long-short CDS strategy.
rationales.B: This reverses the relationship. The modest spread premium belongs to BMS, not LLY: BMS spreads are approximately 10 bps wider than LLY spreads at the roughly 5-year and near-30-year maturities, which is why the market is read as pricing slightly higher credit risk for BMS there.
rationales.C: The curves are closely aligned overall rather than separated by a parallel shift, and the premium is both smaller and localized. The roughly 10 bp BMS concession appears only near the 5-year and 30-year maturities, not as 50 bps across the whole curve. A uniform 50 bp differential between two issuers carrying the same A2/A+ rating would imply a far larger difference in perceived credit risk than the market is pricing.

questions.stem: Bottom-up relative value analysis for two bonds with similar credit risk most likely leads the investor to:

options.A: choose the lower-yielding bond.
options.B: choose the bond with the higher yield spread.
options.C: avoid both bonds.

rationales.A: For two bonds with similar credit risk, taking the lower-yielding one accepts a lower expected excess return for the same exposure. Relative value analysis is precisely the comparison that rules this choice out.
rationales.B: Given two issuers with similar credit risk, the investor will typically choose bonds of the issuer with the higher yield spread, given the greater potential for excess returns. Where the issuers carry different credit-related risk, the comparison is no longer automatic: the investor must decide whether the additional spread is sufficient compensation for the incremental exposure, a judgment captured by the expected excess return calculation, which nets expected credit losses out of the spread earned over the holding period.
rationales.C: Avoiding both bonds forgoes the spread return available from credit exposure. Bottom-up relative value analysis is a tool for choosing between comparable candidates, not a reason to hold neither; a decision to avoid credit altogether would follow from a top-down view on the credit cycle, not from the pairwise comparison here.

drills.los_text: discuss top-down approaches to credit strategies

questions.stem: A top-down credit approach most likely focuses on:

options.A: individual bond issues only.
options.B: individual company financial ratios only.
options.C: a broad set of macro factors.

rationales.A: Selecting among individual bond issues is the scope of the bottom-up approach, which works from the security and issuer upward. A top-down approach starts from the macro environment and works down to sector and rating-category allocation.
rationales.B: Issuer-specific financial ratios such as leverage, coverage and profitability are bottom-up inputs. They inform issuer selection within a sector rather than the sector and rating-category decisions a top-down approach is designed to make.
rationales.C: A top-down approach to credit strategy focuses on a broader set of factors affecting the bond universe, in contrast to the more detailed and issuer-specific bottom-up approach. Macro factors critical to credit investors include economic growth, real rates and inflation, changes in expected market volatility and risk appetite, recent credit spread changes, industry trends, geopolitical risk, and currency movements. Assessment of these factors guides investors in selecting credit market sectors with attractive relative value characteristics, and in choosing among rating categories.

questions.stem: Regarding the link between GDP growth and credit cycle default rates, it is most likely that:

options.A: the relationship holds only for investment-grade issuers.
options.B: sharp declines in GDP growth accompany rising default rates.
options.C: default rates lead GDP declines by several years.

rationales.A: The cyclical default relationship is most pronounced for speculative-grade issuers, not confined to investment-grade ones. Global speculative-grade default rates plotted against G7 real GDP growth from 1962 to 2019 show the clearest cyclical pattern precisely because low-rated issuers have the least capacity to absorb a growth shock; investment-grade default rates move far less over the cycle.
rationales.B: GDP growth is critical to the credit cycle: global speculative-grade default rates plotted against the real GDP growth rate among G7 countries from 1962 to 2019 show that sharp declines in GDP growth are often associated with rising default rates. This is what makes a macro growth view actionable for a credit manager. An above-consensus GDP growth forecast might lead to an increased high-yield allocation, because future defaults would be expected to come in below what the market has priced.
rationales.C: The timing runs the other way: sharp declines in GDP growth are associated with contemporaneous or subsequent increases in default rates, because weaker growth erodes the cash flows that service debt. Defaults do not lead growth declines by several years, so default data cannot be used as a multi-year leading indicator of the macro cycle.

questions.stem: The use of weighted rather than ordinal rating factors across the credit spectrum is most likely motivated by the fact that:

options.A: default risk rises faster as ratings decline than ordinal spacing implies.
options.B: all rating categories warrant identical treatment.
options.C: credit risk does not differ across rating categories.

rationales.A: As investors compare investments across credit ratings, the fact that default risk rises more rapidly as ratings decline is important to consider. The use of weighted factors, such as those established by Moody's based on the likelihood of credit loss over a specific period, rather than ordinal factors across the credit spectrum, enables managers to capture this effect more accurately. The weighted factors run AAA = 1, AA+ = 10, AA = 20, AA- = 40, A+ = 70, A = 120, A- = 180, BBB+ = 260, BBB = 360, BBB- = 610, BB+ = 940, BB = 1,350, and so on. The step from BBB- to BB+ alone is more than 300 factor points, against one step on an ordinal scale, which is why ordinal 1-2-3 spacing understates the risk of lower-rated exposures in a portfolio-weighted average.
rationales.B: Identical treatment of rating categories is the opposite of the point. The weighting scheme exists because rating categories are not equivalent units: the credit loss likelihood attached to each one differs, and by a widening margin as ratings fall.
rationales.C: Credit risk varies dramatically across rating categories. Measured by Moody's weighted factors, the likelihood of credit loss at BB+ (940) is roughly half again that at BBB- (610) and more than five times that at A- (180), so treating the categories as carrying equal risk would misstate portfolio credit exposure.

questions.stem: Research on fixed-income factor investing most likely finds positive risk-adjusted returns to:

options.A: credit rating only.
options.B: carry, defensive, momentum, and value.
options.C: size and value only.

rationales.A: Credit rating is a classification of an issue, not a return factor. A rating category describes where an exposure sits on the credit spectrum; it does not itself constitute a systematic, repeatable source of risk-adjusted excess return of the kind the factor literature documents.
rationales.B: Israel, Palhares and Richardson (2018) found strong evidence of positive risk-adjusted returns to measures of carry, defensive, momentum and value in corporate credit. Carry is the OAS-based expected return earned if the probability of default and the aggregate risk premium are unchanged. Defensive captures the finding that safer, lower-risk assets deliver higher risk-adjusted returns, proxied by market-based leverage, gross profitability and low duration. Momentum is the tendency of bonds with higher recent returns to outperform, measured by trailing six-month excess returns. Value compares low market value against fundamental value, measured as the bond spread less a default probability measure.
rationales.C: Size and value are the classic equity factors. The fixed-income factor evidence is for carry, defensive, momentum and value; size is not among the four, and value alone understates the documented set.

questions.stem: Active credit investors most likely incorporate ESG considerations through:

options.A: random, market-value-weighted issuer selection.
options.B: screens, best-in-class tilts, and ESG-specific funding.
options.C: no explicit treatment of ESG.

rationales.A: Random selection weighted by market value is not an ESG strategy at all; it is closer to passive replication and makes no use of ESG information. The three approaches actually used are exclusionary screens, best-in-class targeting within a sector or rating category, and investments that fund ESG-specific initiatives.
rationales.B: Active credit investors usually incorporate ESG factors into portfolio strategies in one of three basic ways. First, the use of screens either to exclude specific industries with less favorable ESG characteristics, such as firearms, tobacco and coal, or to rule out specific companies or sovereign issuers with ESG-specific ratings below a threshold. Second, the use of ESG ratings to target issuers within a given sector or rating category with relatively favorable ESG characteristics while matching a specific index risk and return. Third, targeting fixed-income investments that directly fund ESG-specific initiatives. ESG ratings and credit ratings tend to be positively correlated.
rationales.C: Ignoring ESG misstates current practice. Adoption in credit is growing and structured, running through exclusionary screens, tilts toward more favorably rated issuers within a sector or rating category, and dedicated mandates that fund specific initiatives; ESG characteristics also correlate positively with credit ratings, so they are not immaterial to credit outcomes.

questions.stem: In the late expansion phase of the credit cycle, credit spreads are most likely:

options.A: unchanged.
options.B: at their tightest levels.
options.C: beginning to widen.

rationales.A: The credit cycle drives systematic changes in spreads, so a phase in which spreads are static is not what late expansion describes. Stable spreads characterize the early expansion phase, when leverage is falling and defaults are coming down from their peak.
rationales.B: Spreads are tightest earlier in the cycle, when leverage is still falling and the default rate is declining from its peak. By late expansion that tightening has run its course and spreads have started to move the other way; the widest levels come later still, in the downturn.
rationales.C: In the late expansion phase, corporate leverage is stable to rising, defaults are rising, credit spreads are rising, and the credit spread slope is steeper for both higher- and lower-rated issuers. Spreads reach their peak in the following downturn phase, not here. The sequence runs: early expansion (falling leverage, defaults falling from their peak, stable spreads, a stable to inverted slope for low-rated issuers), then late expansion (rising leverage, rising defaults, rising spreads, steeper slopes), then downturn (peak leverage, peak defaults, peak spreads), then recovery.

questions.stem: In an economic downturn, high-yield issuers' credit spread curves most likely exhibit:

options.A: Dramatic steepening.
options.B: No change.
options.C: Flattening or inversion.

rationales.A: Dramatic steepening of high-yield spread curves belongs to the recovery and expansion phases, when near-term default risk has largely passed and investors demand compensation mainly for distant, uncertain outcomes. A downturn works in the opposite direction: it concentrates downgrade and default probability in the near term, so short-maturity spreads widen by more than long-maturity spreads and the curve flattens or inverts rather than steepening.
rationales.B: Credit spread curves are reshaped by the cycle rather than held fixed through it. In a downturn, declining issuer profitability flattens investment-grade curves and often inverts high-yield curves, because the near-term probability of downgrade or default jumps while the long end already embeds distress. A curve that did not move with the cycle would imply that the timing of default risk never changes.
rationales.C: High-yield issuers often experience more pronounced flattening, or outright inversion, of the credit spread curve in an economic downturn, because the probability of downgrade or default is higher in the near term than in the long term. Investment-grade and high-yield issuers both face declining profitability in a downturn, but this usually leads to a flatter credit spread curve for investment-grade issuers and often to credit spread curve inversion for high-yield issuers, where the dominant question for the market is survival over the next few quarters rather than the shape of cash flows years out.

questions.stem: In a top-down credit allocation that ranks rating categories by expected excess return net of expected credit loss, the most attractive category to overweight is most likely:

options.A: The highest-rated category.
options.B: The category with the highest expected excess return.
options.C: The lowest-rated category.

rationales.A: The highest-rated category is not automatically the most attractive, because the ranking is done on expected excess return, E[ExcessSpread] ≈ Spread_0 − (EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread) − (POD × LGD), which nets the starting spread and expected spread narrowing against expected credit loss. Category A, with a starting spread of 1.05%, effective spread duration of 5.5, expected spread change of −0.25% and expected loss of 0.06%, gives 1.05% − (5.5 × −0.25%) − 0.06% = 2.37% — the lowest of the four categories. Its credit loss is negligible, but its starting spread is too thin to compete.
rationales.B: The most attractive category is the one with the highest expected excess return, E[ExcessSpread] ≈ Spread_0 − (EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread) − (POD × LGD). Working through the four categories: A: 1.05% − (5.5 × −0.25%) − 0.06% = 2.37%; Baa: 1.35% − (6.0 × −0.35%) − 0.30% = 3.15%; Ba: 2.45% − (4.5 × −0.50%) − 0.60% = 4.10%; B: 3.50% − (4.0 × −0.75%) − 3.00% = 3.50%. Ba has the highest expected excess return at 4.10% and is therefore the rating category to overweight, because it balances a wide starting spread and meaningful expected spread narrowing against a still-modest expected loss. Neither end of the rating scale wins on its own: quality is paid for in forgone spread, and the widest spread is paid for in credit loss.
rationales.C: The lowest-rated category is not automatically the most attractive either. Category B carries the widest starting spread, 3.50%, and the largest expected spread narrowing, −0.75% against an effective spread duration of 4.0, but its expected credit loss of 3.00% consumes the advantage: 3.50% − (4.0 × −0.75%) − 3.00% = 3.50%, below Ba's 4.10%. At the bottom of the rating scale, expected loss rather than spread dominates the expected excess return.
