drills.los_text: discuss liquidity risk in credit markets and how liquidity risk can be managed in a credit portfolio

questions.stem: Corporate bond market liquidity is most likely characterized by:

options.A: A central limit order book with continuous dealer quotes.
options.B: Dealer inventories in over-the-counter markets.
options.C: Centralized exchange trading, as in equities.

rationales.A: Corporate bonds do not trade through an interdealer central limit order book, and dealers carry no obligation to quote continuous two-way prices. Trading is over the counter and traditionally on a request-for-quote basis, with each dealer choosing when, in what size and at what price to supply liquidity. Dealer bond inventories in fact shrank after the 2008-09 regulatory capital requirements, which makes a continuous-quoting obligation still less plausible and is one reason electronic trading platforms grew.
rationales.B: Bonds primarily trade in over-the-counter markets rather than on an exchange. Over-the-counter market liquidity rests with individual dealers — their specific portfolio, the depth of their inventory and their appetite to supply liquidity at a cost. Corporate bonds are traditionally traded on a request-for-quote basis. The use of electronic trading platforms for bond trading has grown because higher regulatory capital requirements reduced bond inventories among dealers after the 2008-09 global financial crisis; as of 2020 those platforms still accounted for less than one-third of individual corporate bond trading volume, while trading in bond portfolios and bond ETFs has grown in importance.
rationales.C: Corporate bond markets are neither centralized nor equity-like in liquidity. A single issuer typically has many outstanding bonds, each trading infrequently and many not at all on a given day, so liquidity rests with individual dealers' inventories and risk appetite rather than with a continuous public order book of the kind equities enjoy.

questions.stem: In estimating the cost of trading a US corporate bond position, TRACE is most likely:

options.A: A US equity exchange listing corporate bonds.
options.B: A real-time transaction reporting system.
options.C: An exchange-traded fund tracking corporate bonds.

rationales.A: TRACE is a reporting system for over-the-counter bond transactions, not a trading venue. Corporate bonds are not listed for order-book trading on a US equity exchange; they trade over the counter, and TRACE exists precisely because that decentralized trading would otherwise leave no public record of price and volume.
rationales.B: TRACE, the Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine, is a separate ex-post liquidity gauge specific to the US corporate bond market. Introduced in 2002, it tracks real-time price and volume reporting for bond transactions. Portfolio managers will often review recent TRACE trading activity to gauge the estimated cost of trading a bond position, since recent prints show where and in what size bonds actually changed hands. It complements the effective spread transaction cost statistic available for actively quoted bonds, and is ex-post in that it reports completed trades rather than quoting a price at which a trade can be done.
rationales.C: TRACE is not an investment product and cannot be bought. It is the Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine, an ex-post transaction reporting facility used to estimate trading costs. Bond ETFs are a separate tool that active credit managers use for liquidity and for quick exposure changes, but they are not what TRACE is.

questions.stem: To manage liquidity risk in an actively managed bond portfolio, a manager is most likely to:

options.A: Trade the most illiquid positions as frequently as possible.
options.B: Avoid fixed-income exposure whenever spreads widen.
options.C: Favor on-the-run issues for short-term tactical positioning.

rationales.A: Trading the most illiquid positions as frequently as possible maximizes the very return erosion the manager is trying to avoid. Illiquid bonds carry the widest bid-ask spreads, so each round trip is most expensive exactly where turnover should be lowest. Illiquid positions are instead reserved for buy-and-hold or strategic positioning, where the holding period is long enough to absorb the entry cost.
rationales.B: Avoiding fixed-income exposure whenever spreads widen is not a liquidity management technique, and spread widening is often when an active credit manager wants to add risk rather than shed it. The technique is to place short-term tactical positions in on-the-run and recently issued bonds, where execution is cheap, while reserving relatively illiquid positions for buy-and-hold strategies.
rationales.C: Active managers will usually favor on-the-run government bonds, or the most recently issued corporate or other bonds, for short-term tactical portfolio positioning, while reserving relatively illiquid positions for buy-and-hold strategies or strategic positioning, in order to minimize expected return erosion from trading costs. Second, they may consider liquid alternatives to individual bond trades to close portfolio gaps where active management adds little value, or to react quickly to rapidly changing markets; those alternatives include CDS and bond ETFs.

questions.stem: Fixed-income ETFs are most likely:

options.A: Actively managed, high-fee products.
options.B: Economic equivalents of direct bond ownership.
options.C: Exchange-traded portfolios with an OTC creation and redemption market.

rationales.A: Most bond ETFs track an index and charge low fees rather than being actively managed at high cost. What distinguishes them is structural rather than fee-related: an over-the-counter primary market in which authorized participants create and redeem shares with the sponsor, and a secondary market in which those shares trade on an exchange. That structure, not active security selection, is what gives the ETF its liquidity.
rationales.B: An ETF share is not economically identical to holding the underlying bonds. Exchange tradability, the creation and redemption mechanism and the unit economics all differ. Because the sponsor targets a specific index or profile, the ETF offers relatively constant portfolio duration — target-maturity ETFs excepted — and pays variable monthly interest based on the overall portfolio, whereas an individual bond rolls down the curve toward a fixed maturity and pays a set coupon. The ETF can also trade at a price away from the value of its holdings.
rationales.C: Fixed-income ETFs are liquid, exchange-traded bond portfolios that create and redeem shares using an over-the-counter primary market existing between a set of institutional investors, or authorized participants, and the ETF sponsor. The ETF shares then trade in the secondary market on an exchange, overcoming the liquidity constraints of individual over-the-counter-traded bonds. Bond ETFs have enjoyed significant growth. Because sponsors target a specific index or profile, ETFs offer relatively constant portfolio duration and pay variable monthly interest based on the overall portfolio. Active credit managers use them to overweight or underweight exposures quickly in rapidly changing markets.

questions.stem: To hedge the benchmark interest rate risk of a long corporate bond position being sold gradually over several weeks, the most appropriate action is most likely to:

options.A: Receive fixed on an asset swap.
options.B: Leave the position unhedged.
options.C: Pay fixed on an asset swap, unwinding it as bonds are sold.

rationales.A: Receiving fixed on the asset swap adds duration to a position that is already long both spread duration and benchmark duration, so it doubles the benchmark interest rate exposure instead of offsetting it. The hedge has to come from the short-duration side of the swap: pay fixed and receive floating.
rationales.B: Leaving the position unhedged retains the full benchmark interest rate risk of the bonds not yet sold, which is precisely the exposure that a slow execution creates. Spread exposure may well be the reason for owning the bonds, but the benchmark rate exposure carried over an extended sale period is separable and can be hedged with a swap while the sale proceeds.
rationales.C: Because the investor's bond position is long both spread duration and benchmark duration, the best hedge is a short-duration, pay-fixed swap rather than a receive-fixed swap. The unwind schedule matters as much as the direction: unwinding the hedge all at once when the bond sale completes would leave the swap standing against bonds already sold, mismatching the hedge against the portion of the position that no longer exists and exposing the investor to benchmark interest rate risk over the sale period. Unwinding the swap in proportion to the amount of the bond sold keeps the offsetting swap position matched to the benchmark interest rate risk of the remaining bond position throughout the execution.

questions.stem: Relative to spreads on liquid bonds, bond dealers' bid-ask spreads on illiquid bonds are most likely:

options.A: Wider.
options.B: Narrower.
options.C: The same.

rationales.A: Dealers cover their costs and earn a profit through the bid-ask spread, so the spread is higher for illiquid bonds that are likely to remain in inventory longer. Dealers often carry inventory because buy and sell orders do not arrive simultaneously, and that inventory has to be financed and its price risk borne; the longer the expected holding period, the more funding and holding cost must be recovered in the quote. Riskier bonds carry wider bid-ask spreads for the same reason, reflecting dealers' aversion to holding them. Government bond spreads are the narrowest of all, and spreads on conventional corporate bonds are narrower than those on complex bonds or bonds with embedded options. Some illiquid bonds will not be quoted at all.
rationales.B: The direction runs the other way: illiquidity widens quoted spreads. A dealer is not compensating the buyer through the quote; the dealer is being compensated for financing and warehousing a position that may take a long time to turn over, and the less liquid the bond, the longer that expected residence in inventory and the wider the quote.
rationales.C: Bid-ask spreads vary systematically with liquidity rather than converging under competitive quoting. Longer expected inventory residence, the financing cost that accompanies it and the price risk borne while the bond sits unsold are all passed into wider quotes. That is why government bonds quote inside conventional corporate bonds, and conventional corporate bonds inside complex or embedded-option issues, and why some illiquid bonds attract no quote at all.

drills.los_text: describe how to assess and manage tail risk in credit portfolios

questions.stem: Tail events are most likely:

options.A: Average market outcomes.
options.B: Uniformly positive outcomes.
options.C: Extreme adverse outcomes beyond those implied by a normal distribution.

rationales.A: Tail events sit in the extremes of the return distribution, not at its center. Average outcomes are described by the body of the distribution and by standard risk measures such as volatility; tail events are what those measures understate, which is why they are addressed through stress testing rather than through the mean.
rationales.B: Tail risk as used in active fixed-income management refers to losses. A distribution has an upper tail as well, but the risk being measured, stress tested and managed is the adverse one: extreme outcomes worse than a normally distributed portfolio would suggest. Nothing about a tail event makes it positive, and the whole point of measuring it is that the loss can exceed what the normal distribution predicts.
rationales.C: Extreme adverse outcomes that exceed those to be expected from a normally distributed portfolio are often referred to as tail events. In the context of active fixed-income management, the measurement and management of tail risk involves stress testing a portfolio's value based on the key fixed-income return factors. Value at risk was introduced for the related purpose of measuring the minimum expected loss over a given period at a specific confidence level, and stress testing complements it by asking what happens in the part of the distribution that the normality assumption handles worst.

questions.stem: A 5% daily VaR of €8.7 million most likely implies:

options.A: A loss of at least €8.7 million on 5% of trading days.
options.B: A maximum possible daily loss of €8.7 million.
options.C: A daily loss of exactly €8.7 million every day.

rationales.A: A 5% daily VaR of €8.7 million implies that a portfolio manager should expect a daily portfolio loss of at least €8.7 million on 5% of all trading days. Assuming normally distributed portfolio returns, the 5% confidence level translates to an outcome at least 1.65 standard deviations below the mean, while a 1% confidence level lies at least 2.33 standard deviations below the mean. Risk managers derive the figure from expected returns, volatilities and correlations using the parametric method, historical simulation or Monte Carlo simulation.
rationales.B: VaR states a minimum loss at a stated probability, not a maximum. On 5% of trading days the loss is at least €8.7 million, and losses within that tail can far exceed the threshold — which is why tail risk is examined separately through stress testing rather than read off the VaR number.
rationales.C: VaR is a probabilistic threshold, not a daily certainty. The €8.7 million figure is the level exceeded on 5% of trading days; on the other 95% the outcome is better than that, and the measure says nothing about what any single day will deliver.

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely a limitation of value at risk (VaR) as a measure of tail risk?

options.A: VaR provides no useful information about a portfolio's risk profile.
options.B: VaR understates the frequency and severity of extreme adverse events.
options.C: VaR fails to capture downside correlation and liquidity risks in market stress.

rationales.A: VaR does provide useful information: it reports the minimum loss expected at a specific confidence level over a specific time period, and its simplicity and transparency are why it is so widely used. Those same qualities become misleading only when VaR is treated as a complete tool for quantifying tail risk, and the limitations are three. First, VaR tends to underestimate the frequency and severity of extreme adverse events. Second, it fails to capture the downside correlation and liquidity risks associated with market stress scenarios. Third, although VaR addresses minimum loss for a specific confidence level, it fails to quantify the average or expected loss under an extreme adverse market scenario. Conditional VaR (CVaR) addresses that last limitation.
rationales.B: This is one of the limitations. VaR is estimated either from distributional assumptions that thin the tails or from a historical period that may contain no severe episode, so both how often and how severely extreme adverse outcomes occur are understated.
rationales.C: This is one of the limitations. In a market stress scenario, correlations among positions rise toward one and bid-ask spreads widen or liquidity disappears entirely, and a VaR estimate parameterised on normal-period data captures neither effect.

questions.stem: For a given time period and confidence level, conditional VaR (CVaR) is best characterized as:

options.A: the same measure of loss as VaR.
options.B: the average loss beyond the VaR threshold.
options.C: the maximum gain expected at a given confidence level.

rationales.A: CVaR and VaR are distinct measures. VaR addresses the minimum loss for a specific confidence level over a specific time period; CVaR takes the losses lying beyond that threshold and averages them. For any loss distribution with mass in the tail, CVaR is therefore larger in magnitude than the VaR struck at the same confidence level, and it answers how severe the tail is rather than where the tail begins.
rationales.B: Conditional value at risk (CVaR), or expected loss, measures the average loss over a specific time period conditional on that loss exceeding the VaR threshold. It is computationally more complex than VaR and is often measured using historical simulation or Monte Carlo techniques. CVaR exists precisely to address VaR's inability to quantify the average or expected loss once the confidence threshold has been breached.
rationales.C: CVaR is defined on the adverse tail of the distribution. It averages the losses conditional on their exceeding the VaR threshold, so it measures loss and has no maximum-gain interpretation; nothing in its construction looks at the favourable side of the distribution.

questions.stem: For a manager considering increasing an overweight allocation to BBB health care, the most appropriate VaR measure is most likely:

options.A: Conditional VaR.
options.B: Relative VaR.
options.C: Incremental VaR.

rationales.A: Conditional VaR measures a portfolio's average loss over a specific time period conditional on that loss exceeding the VaR threshold. It describes the magnitude of tail loss for the portfolio as it stands, and it gives no reading on how one specific position change would alter portfolio risk, which is the decision being taken here.
rationales.B: Relative VaR evaluates all active portfolio positions versus the benchmark index and could be important for an active fixed-income mandate that aims to beat an index once the portfolio change has been made. It reports benchmark-relative risk for the whole active position rather than the marginal effect of the trade under consideration.
rationales.C: Incremental VaR measures the impact of a specific portfolio position change on VaR, which is exactly what a manager weighing a larger overweight in BBB health care needs: the change in portfolio VaR attributable to that single position. Relative VaR evaluates all active positions against the benchmark index, and CVaR measures the portfolio's average loss over a specific time period conditional on that loss exceeding the VaR threshold; neither isolates the effect of the proposed trade.

questions.stem: The three methods most widely used to assess portfolio tail risk are most likely:

options.A: Parametric method, delta-normal mapping, and factor decomposition.
options.B: Historical simulation, stress testing, and incremental VaR.
options.C: Parametric method, historical simulation, and Monte Carlo analysis.

rationales.A: Delta-normal mapping and factor decomposition are not among the three methods; the three are the parametric method, historical simulation, and Monte Carlo analysis. The parametric method is already the approach that assumes a normal distribution for the risk factors, so no separate delta-normal or factor-decomposition method sits alongside it.
rationales.B: Stress testing and hypothetical scenario analyses supplement the three tail-risk methods rather than being one of them, and incremental VaR measures the impact of a specific position change on VaR rather than the shape of the tail. The three methods are the parametric method, historical simulation, and Monte Carlo analysis.
rationales.C: The three methods are: (1) the parametric method, which uses the expected value and standard deviation of the risk factors and assumes a normal distribution, making it simple and transparent but poorly suited to non-normal distributions or option-based portfolios; (2) historical simulation, which prices the existing portfolio using historical parameters and ranks the results, giving actual rather than assumed outcomes and accommodating options, but which is highly dependent on the historical period chosen; and (3) Monte Carlo analysis, which generates random outcomes using portfolio measures and sensitivities, also accommodating options but highly dependent on the model assumptions. Hypothetical scenario analyses often supplement these three methods.

drills.los_text: discuss the use of credit default swap strategies in active fixed-income portfolio management

questions.stem: At credit default swap (CDS) contract inception, the contract's price per unit of par most likely differs from par by:

options.A: the notional amount times the market CDS spread.
options.B: the coupon-spread gap times effective spread duration.
options.C: zero, since inception price is always par.

rationales.A: The CDS price is quoted per unit of par and the upfront payment is expressed as a percentage of notional, so the notional scales the resulting cash amount rather than entering the price relation itself. Multiplying notional by the spread also ignores the fixed coupon, which is what the market spread is measured against, and ignores the effective spread duration over which the coupon-spread difference accrues. The approximation is CDS Price ≈ 1 + ((Fixed Coupon − CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDur_CDS).
rationales.B: CDS Price ≈ 1 + ((Fixed Coupon − CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDur_CDS). If the CDS spread equals the fixed coupon, there is no upfront payment. If the CDS spread is below the fixed coupon, the contract trades at a premium (price above par) and the protection buyer receives ((Fixed Coupon − CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDur_CDS) upfront, in exchange for paying the above-market coupon. If the CDS spread exceeds the fixed coupon, the contract trades at a discount and the protection buyer pays ((CDS Spread − Fixed Coupon) × EffSpreadDur_CDS) upfront.
rationales.C: The price equals par only in the special case where the market CDS spread happens to equal the contract's fixed coupon. Standardised contracts carry fixed coupons — 1.00% for investment grade and 5.00% for high yield — while market spreads move continuously, so the price generally sits above or below par by ((Fixed Coupon − CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDur_CDS), settled as an upfront payment.

questions.stem: A five-year investment-grade CDS contract carries a fixed coupon of 1.00% and trades at a market spread of 0.50%, with an effective spread duration of 4.75. The protection buyer most likely:

options.A: receives 2.375% of notional upfront.
options.B: receives 0.50% of notional upfront.
options.C: pays 2.375% of notional upfront.

rationales.A: Because investment-grade CDS contracts have a fixed coupon of 1.00% p.a. versus the 0.50% p.a. CDS market spread here, the investor buying protection should receive the difference from par upfront in exchange for paying an above-market coupon under the contract. Applying CDS Price ≈ 1 + ((Fixed Coupon − CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDur_CDS), the upfront premium is 2.375% of CDS notional = (1.00% − 0.50%) × 4.75. Standard fixed coupons post-2008 are 1.00% for investment grade and 5.00% for high yield.
rationales.B: The upfront payment is not the market spread itself. It is the gap between the fixed coupon and the market spread, accrued over the contract's effective spread duration: (1.00% − 0.50%) × 4.75 = 2.375% of notional. Taking 0.50% drops the duration multiplier and compares the spread with zero rather than with the 1.00% standard investment-grade coupon.
rationales.C: The direction is reversed. The protection buyer pays upfront only when the market CDS spread exceeds the fixed coupon, because the contract then trades at a discount. Here the 0.50% spread is below the 1.00% standard investment-grade coupon, so the contract trades at a premium and the buyer receives (1.00% − 0.50%) × 4.75 = 2.375% of notional upfront in exchange for paying the above-market coupon.

questions.stem: For a given change in the CDS spread, the change in the CDS price is most likely:

options.A: the spread change times spread duration, with the sign reversed.
options.B: equal to the spread change in both size and sign.
options.C: zero, since price does not respond to spread changes.

rationales.A: Δ(CDS Price) ≈ −(Δ(CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDur_CDS). The spread change is multiplied by the contract's effective spread duration and the sign is reversed, so a widening CDS spread reduces the CDS price while a narrowing spread raises it. Active fixed-income managers rely on this relation when they buy or sell CDS protection across issuers, maturities, and sectors to alter portfolio credit exposure.
rationales.B: Setting the price change equal to the spread change omits both the effective spread duration multiplier and the negative sign. Duration scales the effect — for a five-year contract it is typically between four and five — so a 15 bp widening changes the price by roughly 0.69% of par, not 0.15%, and in the opposite direction to the spread.
rationales.C: CDS prices are highly sensitive to spread changes: Δ(CDS Price) ≈ −(Δ(CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDur_CDS), so the price is unchanged only when the spread is unchanged. With effective spread duration on a five-year contract of roughly 4.5 to 5, even a few basis points of spread movement produces a measurable change in contract value.

questions.stem: A European manager underweights a BBB French media issuer by purchasing protection on €10 million notional of a five-year CDS quoted at 110 bps with an effective spread duration of 4.595. If the issuer's spread widens 15 bps, to 125 bps, the position most likely:

rationales.A: A short risk position gains, rather than loses, when spreads widen. Purchasing protection means paying a premium in exchange for a payment if a credit event occurs, so the contract's value rises as the issuer's credit deteriorates; the manager would lose only if the spread narrowed. The gain here is €68,925 = −€10,000,000 × (−0.15% × 4.595).
rationales.B: The manager can underweight the issuer's credit by purchasing protection in the CDS market, and this short risk position will realise a gain if the issuer's spreads widen. With spreads moving from 110 bps to 125 bps, the change in CDS contract value is estimated by multiplying (−Δ(CDS Spread) × EffSpreadDur_CDS) by the CDS notional: €68,925 = −€10,000,000 × (−0.15% × 4.595).
rationales.C: €150,000 applies the 15 bp spread change to the €10 million notional with no duration multiplier, treating the spread change as a single cash flow rather than as a change in the present value of the remaining premium stream. The spread change must be multiplied by the effective spread duration of 4.595, which gives €68,925.

questions.stem: A credit strategy that an active fixed-income manager can implement in the CDS market is most likely:

options.A: an over-the-counter credit forward.
options.B: an interest rate swap.
options.C: a receiver option on a CDS index.

rationales.A: An over-the-counter forward agreement is a different instrument from a credit default swap: it fixes a price or rate for future delivery rather than transferring credit risk in exchange for a premium, so it is not one of the CDS strategies. The four CDS strategies are single-name CDS, index-based CDS, a payer option on a CDS index, and a receiver option on a CDS index.
rationales.B: Interest rate swaps exchange fixed for floating interest payments and are used to manage duration rather than credit exposure, so they are separate from the CDS market. The four CDS strategies are single-name CDS, index-based CDS, a payer option on a CDS index, and a receiver option on a CDS index.
rationales.C: A receiver option on a CDS index is one of the four CDS strategies: it confers the right to sell protection at a future date, with a payoff of Max(Strike − Credit Spread at expiration, 0) − Option Premium, and it creates a long credit exposure. The other three are single-name CDS, where the protection buyer pays a premium in exchange for a payment if a credit event occurs, giving the buyer a short and the seller a long single-name credit spread position; index-based CDS, which works in the same way across the members of a CDS index, such as the Markit CDX North American Investment Grade index of 125 equally weighted CDS contracts; and a payer option on a CDS index, the right to buy protection at a future date, with a payoff of Max(Credit Spread at expiration − Strike, 0) − Option Premium and a short credit exposure.

questions.stem: A manager purchases protection on a French issuer whose five-year CDS trades at 110 bps with an effective spread duration of 4.697, and sells protection on a German issuer whose five-year CDS trades at 130 bps with an effective spread duration of 4.669, on €10 million notional each. If the French spread widens 10 bps and the German spread narrows 25 bps, the combined result on the two positions is closest to:

rationales.A: The manager purchases protection on the French issuer, a short risk position, and simultaneously sells protection on the German issuer, a long risk position. Short risk (French issuer): €46,970 = −€10,000,000 × (−0.10% × 4.697), a gain because that spread widened. Long risk (German issuer): €116,725 = €10,000,000 × (−(−0.25%) × 4.669), a gain because that spread narrowed. The total gain on the long-short strategy is €163,695 = €46,970 + €116,725.
rationales.B: Both trades are profitable in this scenario, so the combined result cannot be a loss. The short risk French position gains €46,970 as that spread widens 10 bps, and the long risk German position gains €116,725 as that spread narrows 25 bps. A loss would require the French spread to narrow or the German spread to widen.
rationales.C: €46,970 is the gain on the short risk French leg alone, −€10,000,000 × (−0.10% × 4.697), and omits the long risk German leg. Selling protection on the German issuer gains €116,725 = €10,000,000 × (−(−0.25%) × 4.669) as that spread narrows 25 bps, so the two legs together give €163,695.

questions.stem: The most frequently traded CDS index referencing US investment-grade corporate credit is most likely:

options.A: The S&P 500 index.
options.B: The Markit CDX North American Investment Grade index.
options.C: The iTraxx Crossover index.

rationales.A: The S&P 500 is an equity index, not a credit default swap index, so it cannot be a traded CDS index at all. The instrument that references US investment-grade corporate credit is the Markit CDX North American Investment Grade index, built from 125 equally weighted single-name CDS contracts.
rationales.B: The Markit CDX North American Investment Grade index consists of 125 equally weighted CDS contracts on investment-grade entities and includes six subindexes: High Volatility, Consumer Cyclical, Energy, Financials, Industrial, and Telecom, Media and Technology. Across CDS index contracts, the five-year tenor is generally the most frequently traded.
rationales.C: The iTraxx Crossover index references European sub-investment-grade entities, so it is neither a US index nor an investment-grade one. The US investment-grade benchmark is the Markit CDX North American Investment Grade index.

questions.stem: For a credit curve steepening view (expecting near-term default probability to decline), a duration-weighted single-name CDS curve strategy most likely involves:

options.A: Buying short-term protection only.
options.B: Selling short-term protection and buying long-term protection.
options.C: Buying short-term protection and selling long-term protection.

rationales.A: A single short-term leg is not a curve trade: it leaves out the long-term protection purchase that a duration-weighted steepener requires. Without that second leg, the position has no offsetting spread duration, so it is exposed to a parallel move in the whole credit curve rather than to the change in slope the investor has a view on.
rationales.B: An upward-sloping credit curve implies relatively low near-term expected default probability that rises over time. An investor might expect an issuer's CDS curve to steepen if its near-term default probability declines as a result of higher than expected profits and stable leverage. That view is captured by selling short-term protection using a single-name CDS contract and buying long-term protection on the same reference entity. Capitalizing on spread changes for different maturities requires duration matching: the notionals of the two legs, typically the 5-year and the 10-year CDS, are weighted so their spread BPVs offset, leaving the position exposed to the slope of the curve rather than to its level.
rationales.C: Buying short-term protection and selling long-term protection is a curve flattener: it profits if the near-term default probability rises relative to the long term. A steepening view, in which the near-term default probability is declining, requires the opposite legs, namely selling short-term protection and buying long-term protection on the same reference entity.

drills.los_text: discuss various portfolio positioning strategies that managers can use to implement a specific credit spread view

questions.stem: Under a static credit curve view (constant spreads over horizon), the buy-and-hold credit strategy most likely rewards:

options.A: The same return at any spread duration.
options.B: Greater return from higher spread duration.
options.C: Greater return from lower spread duration.

rationales.A: Constant spreads do not equalize returns across spread durations. With an upward-sloping credit curve, bonds of higher spread duration carry wider spreads and roll down that curve as they age, so the manager earns a greater return from the higher spread duration rather than the same return everywhere on the curve.
rationales.B: The first static credit curve strategy involves buying risky bonds with durations above the benchmark without active trading during a subsequent period. If the relationship between long- and short-term credit spreads remains stable over the investment horizon, the manager is rewarded with greater return from the higher spread duration. Rolling down the credit curve generates incremental coupon income, adjusted for any price difference from par, because spreads are wider further out the curve, plus the return that comes from the passage of time.
rationales.C: Lower spread duration earns less of the wider spread available at the long end of an upward-sloping credit curve and gives up roll-down. Under a stable curve it is higher spread duration, not lower, that is rewarded.

questions.stem: An investor holding AUD 50 million face value of a 15-year corporate bond expects stable benchmark yields and credit spreads over the next six months and rolls the position down to 14.5 years. The roll-down produces a total gain of $506,500, comprising $344,000 of price appreciation and $162,500 of coupon income. Of that price appreciation, $217,250 is attributable to the credit spread narrowing from 0.85% to 0.815%, and $75,000 of the coupon income is attributable to the credit spread rather than to the government curve. The portion of the total gain attributable to credit spread roll-down is closest to:

rationales.A: $506,500 is the total roll-down gain, and it combines the government curve and the credit spread contributions: $344,000 of price appreciation plus $162,500 of coupon income. Only $292,250 of that total is estimated to be due to the credit spread curve roll-down, so attributing the whole gain to credit spreads overstates the credit component by $214,250.
rationales.B: The credit component is substantial rather than zero. Of the $506,500 total, $292,250 is estimated to come from the credit spread curve roll-down: $217,250 of price appreciation plus $75,000 of incremental coupon income driven by the credit spread. The government curve accounts for the remaining $214,250.
rationales.C: The total incremental roll-down strategy generates $506,500 (= $344,000 price appreciation + $162,500 coupon income), of which $292,250 (= $217,250 + $75,000) is estimated to be due to the credit spread curve roll-down. The $75,000 is the credit spread portion of the incremental coupon income ($225,000 − $150,000). The $217,250 corresponds to the yield spread narrowing of 0.035%, which is half of the 0.07% total decline in YTM, as the spread falls from 0.85% at 15 years to 0.815% at 14.5 years over the six-month horizon.

questions.stem: For tactical credit spread strategies, a manager expecting widening HY vs IG spreads in an economic slowdown most likely:

options.A: Makes no change to the portfolio.
options.B: Sells high-yield bonds and buys investment-grade bonds.
options.C: Buys high-yield bonds and sells investment-grade bonds.

rationales.A: The view calls for positioning rather than inaction. In cash markets the manager goes short high-yield and long investment-grade; synthetically, the same view is expressed by buying protection on a high-yield CDS index and selling protection on an investment-grade CDS index for the same tenor. Leaving the portfolio unchanged forgoes the expected relative spread widening entirely.
rationales.B: An active manager who expects a weaker economy and a widening of high-yield versus investment-grade credit spread levels can capitalize on this view by buying five-year protection on a high-yield CDS index and selling protection on an investment-grade CDS index for the same tenor. The cash-market equivalent is to go short high-yield bonds and long investment-grade bonds. In a worked illustration of the synthetic version, selling CDX IG protection and buying CDX HY protection, an economic downturn in which investment-grade spreads rise 50% and high-yield spreads double produces a gain of $697,000.
rationales.C: A long high-yield position loses value as high-yield spreads widen, so these legs are backwards for the view. Because high-yield spreads are expected to widen by more than investment-grade spreads, the profitable positioning is short high-yield and long investment-grade, or synthetically buying protection on the high-yield index and selling protection on the investment-grade index.

questions.stem: A manager compares an equally weighted portfolio of A, Baa, Ba and B rated corporate bonds with a tactical portfolio that holds 33.3% Ba, 33.3% B, and the remaining 33.3% split evenly between A and Baa. If credit spreads and expected loss rates both fall by one-third over the horizon, the tactical portfolio most likely:

options.A: Outperforms the equally weighted portfolio.
options.B: Underperforms the equally weighted portfolio.
options.C: Matches the equally weighted portfolio.

rationales.A: With spreads and expected loss rates falling by one-third, expected returns by rating are A 3.898%, Baa 5.80%, Ba 8.705% and B 9.832%. The passive equally weighted portfolio returns 7.059% = (3.898% + 5.80% + 8.705% + 9.832%)/4. The tactical portfolio, at 33.3% Ba, 33.3% B and the remaining third split between A and Baa, returns 7.795% = 3.898%/6 + 5.80%/6 + 8.705%/3 + 9.832%/3. The overweight to high yield captures more of the recovery's spread compression, so the tactical portfolio outperforms by about 0.74 percentage points.
rationales.B: The tactical portfolio outperforms rather than lags: 7.795% against 7.059% for the equally weighted portfolio. Underperformance would require the lower-rated bonds it overweights to do worse, which is what happens when spreads widen, not when spreads and expected loss rates fall by a third.
rationales.C: A recovery benefits the lower-rated tranches differentially, since Ba and B spreads compress by far more in absolute terms than A and Baa spreads do. A portfolio tilted toward them therefore does not match the equally weighted portfolio: it returns 7.795% against 7.059%.

questions.stem: An investor expecting an economic recovery, with the five-year CDX HY index at 450 bps and the 10-year CDX HY index at 375 bps, implements a duration-neutral CDX HY curve steepener. The strategy most likely involves:

options.A: Selling protection at both maturities.
options.B: Selling five-year protection and buying 10-year protection.
options.C: Buying protection at both maturities.

rationales.A: Selling protection on both maturities is a directional long-credit position: the spread BPVs of the two legs add rather than offset, so the position is neither duration-neutral nor a curve trade, and it would gain or lose on a parallel move in high-yield spreads.
rationales.B: The appropriate strategy is to sell protection on the five-year CDX HY and buy protection on the 10-year CDX HY, which capitalizes on the expected steepening as the five-year spread declines by more than the 10-year spread. The five-year notional is scaled to match the BPV of the 10-year leg: (EffSpreadDur 10y / EffSpreadDur 5y) × $10 million = (8.656/4.637) × $10 million = $18,667,000. For a 175 bp fall in the five-year spread and a 25 bp fall in the 10-year spread, the five-year leg gains $1,514,780 and the 10-year leg loses $216,400, for a net portfolio gain of $1,298,380.
rationales.C: Buying protection on both maturities takes the same direction on each leg, so it is neither duration-neutral nor a steepener. It is a directional short-credit position that profits from spread widening, the opposite of the expected recovery.

questions.stem: For a credit spread carry-and-roll-down strategy to be effective, the manager must most likely assume that:

options.A: credit spreads move dramatically.
options.B: credit spreads and benchmark yields remain stable.
options.C: benchmark yields rise while credit spreads remain stable.

rationales.A: Stability, not movement, is the key assumption. Carry and roll-down returns come from earning the coupon and from the bond rolling to a point of lower spread on an unchanged curve. Dramatic spread movement is what disrupts the strategy: if spreads widen unexpectedly during the investment horizon, the position experiences unrealized losses.
rationales.B: Static credit curve strategies, buy-and-hold and carry-and-roll-down alike, require the assumption of stable benchmark yields and credit spreads over the horizon. The investor who expects stable benchmark yields and credit spreads over, for example, the next six months earns the carry plus the price gain from rolling down a curve that has not moved. If spreads widen unexpectedly during that horizon, the position experiences unrealized losses, so deviations from the static assumption are the source of risk in the strategy.
rationales.C: Rising benchmark yields would generate price losses on the position. Carry-and-roll-down requires stable benchmark yields as well as stable credit spreads over the horizon.

questions.stem: To add credit spread duration or increase credit exposure using derivatives, a manager is most likely to:

options.A: buy cash bonds only, avoiding derivatives.
options.B: sell single-name or index CDS protection at longer maturities or lower credit quality.
options.C: buy single-name or index CDS protection.

rationales.A: Derivatives are a standard route to added spread duration, so avoiding them entirely is unnecessary. Selling CDS single-name or index protection for longer maturities or lower credit quality adds credit exposure without buying cash bonds, and a long-short approach achieves a similar objective.
rationales.B: Derivative-based credit strategies to add credit spread duration or increase credit exposure include selling CDS single-name or index protection for longer maturities or lower credit quality, or using a long-short approach to achieve a similar objective. Selling protection creates long risk exposure, analogous to owning the bonds, while buying protection creates short risk exposure, analogous to shorting them.
rationales.C: Buying protection reduces credit exposure: it is a short risk position, analogous to shorting the bonds. Selling protection is what adds credit exposure and spread duration.

drills.los_text: discuss considerations in constructing and managing portfolios across international credit markets

questions.stem: An investor holds a US corporate bond portfolio, equally weighted across A, Baa, Ba and B rated issuers, that returns 3.30%, and adds an iTraxx-Xover position weighted at one-half of the US portfolio. The iTraxx-Xover position returns 4.077% in euro terms, and the euro appreciates 1% against the US dollar over the period. The total portfolio return in US dollars is closest to:

rationales.A: 1.5% reflects only a currency-sized return and ignores both the 3.30% earned on the US corporate bond portfolio and the credit return on the iTraxx-Xover position, which together give 5.86%.
rationales.B: 3.30% is the return on the US corporate bond portfolio alone. It leaves out the iTraxx-Xover contribution, which adds 5.118%/2 = 2.559% because the position carries a weight equal to one-half of the US portfolio.
rationales.C: The return on the equally weighted US portfolio is 3.30%. The US dollar return on the iTraxx-Xover position is 5.118% = (1 + 4.077%) × (1 + 1.00%) − 1, applying R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1. Given that iTraxx-Xover carries a weight equal to one-half of the US corporate bond portfolio, the strategy returns 5.86% = 3.30% + 5.118%/2. The 4.077% euro-denominated gain on the five-year iTraxx-Xover position itself comes from (1.085 − 1.0425)/1.0425.

questions.stem: The inputs to the Bloomberg Sovereign Risk (SRSK) model, which estimates a sovereign issuer's one-year probability of default, are most likely:

options.A: quantitative and qualitative factors combined.
options.B: political risk alone.
options.C: historical default rates alone.

rationales.A: The SRSK model combines quantitative and qualitative factors — external debt to GDP, currency reserves, GDP growth, and political risk — to estimate a sovereign issuer's one-year probability of default. As with the DRSK model used for corporate issuers, users can change the model inputs, and the model also derives a model CDS spread that can be compared with the market CDS spread as a check on whether the sovereign's traded credit protection looks rich or cheap against fundamentals. Applied to Costa Rica, the model produced a one-year default risk estimate of 1.28%.
rationales.B: Political risk is one factor among several. External debt to GDP, currency reserves, and GDP growth sit alongside it in the model, and those macro-financial variables carry most of the estimate. A model driven by political risk alone could not distinguish a politically fragile sovereign with low external debt and ample reserves from one with the same politics and no capacity to pay.
rationales.C: The model is forward-looking: it combines current quantitative macro-financial variables with qualitative factors rather than extrapolating past sovereign defaults forward. Sovereign defaults are rare enough that a purely historical frequency would be a thin basis for an estimate, and it would ignore the issuer's present debt burden, reserve position, and growth outlook, which are exactly what the model reads.

questions.stem: The ratio most appropriate for assessing a sovereign borrower's ability to meet interest payments on its US dollar-denominated bonds over the next 12 months is most likely:

options.A: External debt/GDP.
options.B: Currency reserves/GDP.
options.C: Government budget deficit/GDP.

rationales.A: The external debt-to-GDP ratio is a measure of financial leverage to foreign lenders: the stock of obligations owed abroad relative to the size of the economy. It is a solvency measure, not a liquidity measure, and it says nothing about whether the foreign currency needed for the next twelve months of coupon payments is actually on hand. A heavily indebted sovereign with large reserves and a lightly indebted one with none can both look manageable on this ratio while differing entirely in near-term capacity to pay.
rationales.B: Currency reserves as a percentage of GDP measure the liquidity available in foreign currency to meet external obligations, which is precisely what short-term servicing of dollar-denominated debt requires. Because the bonds are denominated in US dollars, the sovereign must hold US dollars or other convertible foreign currency to pay the coupons; capacity to raise domestic currency through taxation or domestic issuance does not substitute for it. By contrast, the government budget deficit as a percentage of GDP is a gauge of fiscal stability for the domestic economy, and the external debt-to-GDP ratio measures financial leverage to foreign lenders — neither captures near-term foreign currency liquidity.
rationales.C: The government budget deficit as a percentage of GDP gauges fiscal stability in the domestic economy: whether current spending is being financed on a sustainable path. It is denominated in the wrong terms for this question. A sovereign can run a small deficit and still lack the foreign currency needed to pay a dollar coupon next quarter, and a sovereign running a large deficit financed in domestic currency may hold ample reserves, so the ratio does not address short-term external liquidity.

questions.stem: The sovereign ceiling is most likely:

options.A: a cap on a company's rating at the rating of its domicile's sovereign.
options.B: a cap on all corporate credit spreads.
options.C: a statutory limit on US federal debt.

rationales.A: The sovereign ceiling is the convention, applied to corporate issuers globally, that a company's rating is typically no higher than the sovereign credit rating of its domicile. It helps explain why credit quality in the emerging market credit universe shows a high concentration in the lower investment-grade and upper high-yield rating categories: that concentration largely reflects the sovereign ratings of emerging markets themselves, and the ceiling carries those sovereign ratings through to the corporates domiciled there. A strong exporter earning hard-currency revenue can therefore be rated below its standalone credit quality simply because of where it is domiciled.
rationales.B: The ceiling is expressed in ratings, not in spreads. It places no upper bound on where a corporate bond can trade: spreads on issuers domiciled in a weakening sovereign routinely widen well beyond the sovereign's own spread, and nothing in a rating convention prevents that. Treating it as a spread cap would also imply a price ceiling the market has no mechanism to enforce.
rationales.C: The US federal debt limit is a statutory borrowing cap set by Congress on the US government's own obligations and is unrelated to this concept. The sovereign ceiling is a rating agency convention that links the ratings of corporate issuers to the rating of their home sovereign, and it applies to issuers globally rather than to any one government's borrowing authority.

questions.stem: Emerging markets are most likely characterized by:

options.A: volatile growth, capital controls, and elevated geopolitical risk.
options.B: lower growth, stable credit fundamentals, and IMF support.
options.C: dollar-pegged currencies and negligible currency risk.

rationales.A: Emerging markets are characterized by higher, more volatile, and less balanced economic growth than developed markets, often together with greater geopolitical risk, currency restrictions, and capital controls. Sovereign credit risk is therefore a critical starting point in considering fixed-income investments in emerging markets, where both the ability and the willingness of issuers to repay debt matter. Institutional considerations sit alongside the macro-financial data in that assessment: political stability, transparency, and adherence to property rights and contract law.
rationales.B: Emerging market growth is typically higher than developed market growth, not lower, and it is also more volatile and less balanced. Credit fundamentals are correspondingly less stable rather than more: greater geopolitical risk, currency restrictions, and capital controls all work against stability. IMF support programs are a response to stress rather than evidence of its absence, and the conditionality attached to them can itself disrupt an issuer's operating environment and cash flows.
rationales.C: Emerging market currencies are often highly volatile, and currency restrictions and capital controls add to foreign exchange risk rather than remove it. Dollar pegs are not universal across emerging markets, and where they exist they are not permanent. Temporary deviations from a fixed exchange rate are possible under such regimes, but what is more common during economic crises is exchange rate regime change, central bank intervention, and/or outright devaluation — the moments when the currency exposure matters most are exactly when the peg is least reliable.

questions.stem: Emerging market currency risk is most likely:

options.A: eliminated by holding US dollar-denominated debt.
options.B: offset by interest rate parity.
options.C: amplified by restrictive currency and derivative markets.

rationales.A: Holding US dollar-denominated emerging market debt removes direct exchange rate exposure on the bond's cash flows, but it does not eliminate currency considerations. Local currency weakness still pressures the issuer's capacity to service external debt out of local currency revenue, so the credit risk of the dollar bond rises precisely when the currency falls — the exposure reappears as default risk rather than translation risk. Local-currency emerging market debt, for its part, carries significant foreign exchange risk directly.
rationales.B: Higher yields to maturity available in emerging market currencies do typically suggest that those currencies will depreciate over time, which is what uncovered interest rate parity implies. Parity does not hold reliably, however. Divergence from it — the forward rate bias — is common enough that investors deliberately seek to exploit it by investing in higher-yielding currencies, and realized depreciation can be either smaller or far larger than parity implies. During crises, exchange rate regime change, central bank intervention, and devaluation can produce moves no yield premium compensates, so the yield advantage is not an offset.
rationales.C: Currency volatility can be particularly significant in emerging markets as a result of restrictive currency regimes and derivative markets. Higher yields to maturity available in emerging market currencies versus developed markets typically suggest that these currencies will depreciate over time, consistent with interest rate parity. That said, emerging markets also offer investors the opportunity to exploit divergence from interest rate parity conditions, known as the forward rate bias, by investing in the higher-yielding currencies. Although temporary deviations from a fixed exchange rate are possible under such regimes, what is more common during economic crises is exchange rate regime change, central bank intervention, and/or devaluation.

questions.stem: For a US-based investor choosing between an emerging market issuer's local-currency bond, with the higher yield to maturity, and the same issuer's US dollar-denominated bond, with the lower yield to maturity, the choice most likely depends on:

options.A: the issuer's credit risk alone.
options.B: the yield gap and the expected currency depreciation.
options.C: the yield-to-maturity differential alone.

rationales.A: The issuer is the same for both bonds, so there is no difference in issuer credit risk to choose between. What distinguishes the two instruments is the currency of denomination, and the decision therefore weighs the yield-to-maturity gap in favour of the local currency bond against the local currency's expected depreciation versus the US dollar over the investment horizon.
rationales.B: A US-based investor seeking to maximize US dollar-denominated return must consider the relationship between the higher local currency bond yield to maturity, the lower US dollar bond yield to maturity, and the local currency's expected depreciation (or appreciation) versus the US dollar over the investment horizon. Uncovered interest rate parity suggests that local currency depreciation against the US dollar would offset any benefit of the higher yield to maturity. An investor with a bullish view of the emerging economy's growth prospects, however, would benefit from the forward rate bias and earn a higher return in US dollar terms from an unhedged investment in the local currency bond, provided the local currency depreciates by less than parity implies.
rationales.C: The yield-to-maturity differential is only one side of the comparison. The higher local yield can be entirely consumed, or more than consumed, by depreciation of the local currency against the US dollar over the holding period, which is what uncovered interest rate parity implies will happen on average. A view on the exchange rate is therefore essential rather than optional, and it is that view, not the yield gap by itself, that decides the choice.

drills.los_text: describe the use of structured financial instruments as an alternative to corporate bonds in credit portfolios

questions.stem: Among the categories of structured financial instruments that offer an alternative to corporate bonds, the one least likely to be included is:

options.A: mortgage-backed securities, asset-backed securities, and covered bonds.
options.B: individual corporate bonds.
options.C: collateralized debt and collateralized loan obligations.

rationales.A: All three are structured categories. Mortgage-backed securities are claims on a commercial or residential mortgage pool; asset-backed securities are backed by credit card, auto, and other consumer loans; covered bonds are senior debt obligations backed by a pool of real estate or public sector assets, with dual recourse to both the issuing financial institution and the asset pool.
rationales.B: Individual corporate bonds are not structured instruments — they are the alternative that structured products offer diversification from. The five structured categories are: collateralized debt obligations, backed by a diversified pool of debt; collateralized loan obligations, backed by a diversified pool of floating-rate leveraged loans; mortgage-backed securities, backed by a commercial or residential mortgage pool; asset-backed securities, backed by credit card, auto, and other loans; and covered bonds, senior debt backed by real estate or public sector assets with dual recourse.
rationales.C: Both are structured categories. A collateralized debt obligation is backed by a diversified pool of debt and a collateralized loan obligation by a diversified pool of floating-rate leveraged loans. In each case a special purpose vehicle owns the underlying pool and issues debt in tranches against the pool's cash flows, which is what makes the instrument structured rather than a direct claim on an operating company.

questions.stem: Structured products most likely offer active credit managers:

options.A: lower returns than comparably rated corporate bonds.
options.B: no benefit beyond that of corporate bonds.
options.C: access to new cash-flow pools and tranched credit exposure.

rationales.A: Tranche selection and the structural leverage embedded in subordination can enhance returns relative to comparably rated corporate bonds rather than depress them. An active investor who takes a lower-rated tranche is paid for absorbing a greater proportion of the pool's default risk, and exposure to interest rate volatility through mortgage prepayment and extension risk is itself a compensated exposure. Structuring and servicing costs exist, but they do not systematically consume the yield available from the underlying collateral.
rationales.B: Structured instruments give access to fixed-income cash flows that corporate bonds do not reach — commercial and residential real estate, credit card, auto, and other consumer loans — so their risk-return profile is not that of the issuing institutions' senior unsecured debt. Securitization moves those assets into a special purpose vehicle and redistributes their default risk across tranches, which is precisely what makes the exposure distinct and what lets a manager tailor it.
rationales.C: Structured financial instruments can offer active credit managers the ability to access fixed-income cash flows such as commercial or residential real estate and consumer loans, enhance returns by increasing portfolio exposure to interest rate volatility via mortgage prepayment and extension risk, and add debt exposure created by the redistribution of default risk into different tranches across the credit spectrum.

questions.stem: Tranching in asset-backed security and collateralized debt obligation transactions most likely:

options.A: gives every tranche the same risk.
options.B: eliminates default risk from the structure.
options.C: concentrates default risk in the lower-rated tranches.

rationales.A: Stratification of risk is the point of tranching. Senior tranches are protected by the subordination of everything beneath them, while the lower tranches absorb losses first, so the tranches differ in credit risk and therefore in rating — not merely in coupon convention. That difference is what allows an active investor to overweight default risk with a lower-rated tranche or underweight it with a higher-rated one.
rationales.B: Default risk is redistributed across the capital structure, not eliminated. Losses on the underlying asset pool still arrive in full; tranching determines only the order in which the holders of each claim bear them. Internal credit enhancement and overcollateralization reduce the risk borne by the senior tranches precisely by increasing the risk borne by the junior ones, so the total risk in the structure is unchanged.
rationales.C: Tranching establishes higher-rated tranches via internal credit enhancement or overcollateralization, with successively lower-rated tranches absorbing a greater proportion of the associated default risk. The issuer is a special purpose vehicle that owns the underlying asset pool and issues debt across several tranches backed by the pool's cash flows. An active investor might overweight default risk by choosing a lower-rated tranche based on a tactical view, or alternatively underweight credit exposure by using a higher-rated tranche in a downturn.

questions.stem: Covered bonds differ from asset-backed securities most likely because they:

options.A: offer dual recourse and asset substitution.
options.B: offer no recourse to the issuing institution.
options.C: offer the highest yield among secured instruments.

rationales.A: Covered bonds offer real estate cash flow exposure similar to that of asset-backed securities, but they carry dual recourse — to both the issuing financial institution and the underlying asset pool — as well as the substitution of non-performing assets out of the cover pool. Those two features mean covered bonds usually involve lower credit risk and a lower yield than a comparable asset-backed security. They are senior debt obligations backed by a pool of commercial or residential mortgages or public sector assets.
rationales.B: Dual recourse — to the issuing financial institution and to the underlying asset pool — is the covered bond's defining feature, so recourse to the issuer is present rather than absent. It is the asset-backed security, issued by a special purpose vehicle that owns the pool outright and is bankruptcy-remote from the originator, where the investor's claim stops at the collateral.
rationales.C: The stronger protections of a covered bond typically produce a lower yield, not the highest. Dual recourse and the substitution of non-performing assets reduce credit risk relative to an asset-backed security backed by the same kind of collateral, and investors accept less yield in exchange for that reduction.

questions.stem: For a manager anticipating a decline in residential housing prices, the most appropriate structured product trade is most likely a shift:

options.A: from BBB rated to A rated MBS tranches.
options.B: from A rated to BB rated credit card ABS tranches.
options.C: from BBB rated to A rated CDO tranches.

rationales.A: As the housing sector slows and default rates rise, credit spreads of lower-rated MBS tend to widen by more than those of higher-rated MBS. Moving from a BBB rated to an A rated MBS tranche keeps the investor exposed to real estate cash flows while reducing exposure to that spread widening, so it targets the housing view directly rather than taking general credit risk off the table.
rationales.B: A move from an A rated to a BB rated credit card ABS tranche increases credit exposure, the wrong direction for a manager who expects rising defaults and widening spreads. It also sits in consumer receivables rather than residential mortgages, so it does not express a housing view at all.
rationales.C: Moving from BBB rated to A rated CDO tranches does reduce overall credit and market risk, but CDO collateral is not specific to residential mortgages. The trade is a general up-in-quality move, not the targeted MBS expression of a housing price decline.

questions.stem: For a manager anticipating an economic recovery with rising short-term rates and a flatter benchmark yield curve, the most appropriate structured product trade is most likely a shift:

options.A: from an A rated CDO tranche to a BBB rated CLO tranche.
options.B: from MBS into covered bonds.
options.C: from BB rated to A rated auto ABS tranches.

rationales.A: Economic recovery is typically associated with lower defaults and greater credit spread tightening among lower-rated issuers and debt tranches, so moving from A to BBB captures that spread compression. CLO tranches also benefit more than CDO tranches from a rise in short-term rates, because CLOs comprise leveraged loans priced off market reference rates plus a credit spread. The shift therefore captures both the lower-rated credit spread compression and the floating-rate reference rate benefit.
rationales.B: Covered bonds carry dual recourse to the issuer and to the cover pool, so replacing MBS with them reduces credit risk. That is the wrong direction for a recovery view, and as fixed-rate instruments they also leave the portfolio with no way to benefit from the rise in short-term rates.
rationales.C: Moving from a BB rated to an A rated auto ABS tranche reduces credit exposure, which limits the benefit from the spread tightening a recovery brings to lower-rated tranches. It also adds no floating-rate exposure, so nothing in the trade gains from rising short-term rates.

drills.los_text: describe key inputs, outputs, and considerations in using analytical tools to manage fixed-income portfolios

questions.stem: The primary inputs for fixed-income analytical models most likely include:

options.A: real-time market data feeds only.
options.B: all cash bond, derivative, repo, and cash positions across currencies.
options.C: cash bond positions only.

rationales.A: Position-level data is a required input, not something the model infers. Market data feeds are used to value positions, but the positions themselves must be supplied, each security identified by CUSIP or ISIN; models do not read holdings out of custodial records.
rationales.B: Primary inputs for fixed-income models include all long and short cash bond and derivative positions, repurchase agreements, and cash across currencies. Fixed-income security inputs use CUSIP or ISIN identifiers to capture all relevant features, such as interest and principal payment dates, day count conventions, and put-call features. Portfolio derivative and repo position inputs also include details of those agreements, such as settlement dates, option strike prices, and collateral terms necessary to satisfy derivative counterparty or clearing requirements as markets change.
rationales.C: Derivatives, repurchase agreements, and cash across currencies belong in the position inputs alongside cash bonds. Derivative and repo inputs carry settlement dates, strike prices, and collateral terms precisely because the analytical model, not the settlement system, has to value and risk-manage those exposures.

questions.stem: Real-time market data feeds from vendors most likely include:

options.A: exchange rates only.
options.B: equity prices only.
options.C: rates, credit curves, implied volatilities, and exchange rates.

rationales.A: Exchange rates are only one element of the feed. Spot and forward rates, credit curves, and implied volatilities all flow through the same vendor interfaces; none of them is sourced manually in a production analytics platform.
rationales.B: Equity prices alone cannot value a bond portfolio. Fixed-income models need spot and forward rates, credit curves, implied volatilities, and exchange rates to price positions and measure risk.
rationales.C: Real-time market data feeds, usually sourced from vendors via application programming interfaces, include spot and forward rates, credit curves, implied volatilities, and exchange rates that are used to value historical, existing, and potential future new portfolio positions. These tools value inactively traded fixed-income instruments using matrix pricing (or evaluated pricing) based on observable liquid benchmark yields to maturity of similar maturity and duration and credit spreads of actively traded bonds with comparable times to maturity, credit quality, and sector. Additional model inputs include index subscriptions, ESG and credit ratings, and issuer balance sheet data.

questions.stem: Compared with more static equity indexes, fixed-income indexes are most likely to:

options.A: change only through ratings migration.
options.B: change constantly with issuance, maturities, ratings changes, calls, and prepayments.
options.C: stay static between annual reconstitutions.

rationales.A: Ratings migration is one source of change, but not the only one. Matured bonds leave the index rather than remaining in it at a final price, and new debt issuance, calls, and prepayments all move index membership as well.
rationales.B: In contrast to more static equity indexes, fixed-income indexes are subject to constant change as a result of both new debt issuance and bond maturities as well as ratings changes, bond callability, and prepayment. This is a key differentiator between fixed-income and equity index management and a critical consideration in analytical models: as new bonds are issued and old ones mature or are called or prepaid, index composition shifts continuously, so benchmark exposures drift even when the manager does not trade.
rationales.C: Bond indexes change continuously rather than only at a scheduled reconstitution. Issuance, maturities, ratings migration, calls, and prepayments all move membership between rebalancing dates, which is precisely what distinguishes them from more static equity indexes.

questions.curriculum_ref: Analytical Tools — FI vs equity indexes

questions.stem: Model assumptions in fixed-income analytical tools most likely include:

options.A: parameters standardized by regulators.
options.B: user-defined parameters such as the term structure model and the VaR methodology.
options.C: vendor-supplied market data only.

rationales.A: Parameters are user-defined rather than standardized by regulators for comparability. The manager chooses the term structure model, the investment time horizon, the VaR methodology, the historical or specific market scenarios, and the portfolio filters, which is why two managers holding the same positions can reach different portfolio outcomes.
rationales.B: Model assumptions include user-defined parameters such as term structure models, investment time horizon, VaR methodology, historical and/or specific market scenarios, and portfolio filters that could involve inclusion or exclusion of specific sectors or a minimum ESG rating threshold for consideration. Different assumptions can lead to different portfolio outcomes.
rationales.C: Vendor market data is an input to the model, not an assumption of it. The assumptions are the user-defined choices layered on top of that data: the term structure model, the investment horizon, the VaR methodology, the scenarios run, and the sector or ESG filters applied.

questions.stem: The outputs of fixed-income analytical models most likely support:

options.A: ratings surveillance only.
options.B: every stage of the active management process.
options.C: portfolio construction only.

rationales.A: Ratings surveillance is a narrow slice of what the outputs cover. They span the full active management workflow: portfolio selection and construction, risk analysis of existing and prospective positions, and trading and position management.
rationales.B: Fixed-income analytical model outputs support each stage of the active portfolio management process, namely portfolio selection and construction, risk analysis of existing and prospective portfolio positions, and trading and position management. A portfolio summary or landing page typically aggregates current portfolio risk and return across sectors, ratings, and currencies versus the benchmark index, and the applications supporting research and portfolio construction let managers assess the expected change in portfolio performance from adding incremental long or short positions.
rationales.C: Risk analysis of existing and prospective positions is a core output alongside construction, as is trading and position management. Risk is measured inside the same tools, not handled outside them.
